# evalpheno <img src="fig/evalpheno.png" align="right" height="138" alt="" />

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.15174551.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15174551)
<!-- badges: end -->

`evalpheno` lets you construct temperature-driven phenology models, set their
parameters, and simulate variation among individual buds. Models combine
chill and heat accumulation with sequential, parallel, partial-overlap or
PhenoFlex structures.

## Installation

Install the development version from GitHub:

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("larscaspersen/eval_phenoflex")
```

## Construct a model

Choose a model structure and the chill and heat submodels:

```{r construct}
library(evalpheno)

model <- pheno_model()
```

By default, `pheno_model()` constructs a PhenoFlex model with the Dynamic Model
for chill accumulation and the Growing Degree Hour Model for heat accumulation.
You can select other model structures using `"sequential"`, `"parallel"` or
`"partial_overlap"`.

You can visualize the model structure:

```{r plot-structure, }
plot(model)
```

Use `parameter_schema()` to view the model parameters and their descriptions:

```{r table-schema-plain, eval=FALSE}
parameter_schema(model)
```

```{r table-schema, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  parameter_schema(model),
  format = "html",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```


Supply model parameters as a **named** vector when constructing the model, or
adjust them afterward:

```{r adjust-par}
model$parameters['yc'] <- 80

print(model)
```



Alternative chill submodels are `chill_hours()`, `chill_utah()` and
`chill_positive_utah()`. `chill_none()` creates a heat-only model, bypassing
chill-dependent coupling. Chill-hours thresholds and Utah zone weights appear
in the parameter schema and can be calibrated. User-defined chill submodels can be supplied through `chill_custom()`.

## Predict bloom dates

Prepare hourly temperature time series to predict bloom dates. The
[chillR package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/chillR/index.html)
[@luedelingChillRStatisticalMethods2024] provides tools for acquiring and
processing temperature data:

```{r process-weather}
data("KA_weather", package = "chillR")
hourly <- chillR::stack_hourly_temps(
  KA_weather, latitude = 50.4)$hourtemps
seasons <- chillR::genSeasonList(hourly, mrange = c(8, 6), years = 1999:2009)
names(seasons) <- as.character(1999:2009)
```



```{r predict}
model <- pheno_model(parameters = c(yc = 40, zc = 250))

predict_phenology(model, seasons)
```

## Visualize the processes

Plot chill and heat accumulation and the transition between them:

```{r model-plots}
plot_processes(model, seasons, ribbon = TRUE)
```

`plot_processes()` shows chill accumulation, the transition, and effective heat
over time. With a season list, grey curves show individual seasons and black
curves show pointwise medians. A dot marks the median bloom date, with whiskers
spanning the earliest and latest successful predictions. Set `ribbon = TRUE`
to replace the individual curves with a shaded range from the minimum to the
maximum. Partial-overlap models show their changing heat requirement in the
transition panel; heat-only models show
just heat accumulation.


## Calibrate model parameters

Use `fit_phenology()` to calibrate the model parameters. Only the parameters
specified in the lower and upper bounds are adjusted. Install the
[DEoptim package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DEoptim/index.html)
[@deoptim_package_2011, @ardia_differential_2011] to use the default optimizer.
Alternatively, install the
[GenSA package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GenSA/index.html)
[@xiang_generalized_2013] and supply `optimizer = "GenSA"` in the function call.

```{r}
require(DEoptim)
model <- pheno_model()
lower <- c(yc = 10)
upper <- c(yc = 80)

# Replace these synthetic predictions with observed bloom dates.
observed <- predict_phenology(model, seasons)

# Run the optimizer. Use more iterations for actual calibrations.
fit <- fit_phenology(model, evaluation = phenology_rss, observed = observed,
                     seasons = seasons, lower, upper, seed = 17, max_iterations = 2)

print(fit)

```
## Model a bud population

Share chill and potential heat accumulation across buds while allowing their
requirements to vary:

```{r population}
population <- population_pheno_model(
  structure = "phenoflex", n = 100,
  sd = c(yc = 2, zc = 10), seed = 17
)
means <- model_parameters(population)
means[c("yc", "zc")] <- c(40, 250)

buds <- predict_population_phenology(population, seasons[[1]], parameters = means)
quantile(buds$bloom_jday, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), na.rm = TRUE)
```

Population models also support cutting and constant-temperature forcing experiments.

Read the [online guide](https://larscaspersen.github.io/eval_phenoflex/) for
full workflows, with chapters on
[Getting started](https://larscaspersen.github.io/eval_phenoflex/getting-started.html),
[Model structures and submodels](https://larscaspersen.github.io/eval_phenoflex/model-structures-and-submodels.html),
[Model calibration](https://larscaspersen.github.io/eval_phenoflex/model-calibration_special-cases.html), and
[Bud populations](https://larscaspersen.github.io/eval_phenoflex/bud-population.html).
